title: Helping Your Child Buy a Home

chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.html:
More and more parents help their child get into homeownership. It's a lovely gesture — one that deserves to be structured to protect everyone. Gift, loan, co-signing: each option has its implications.

This guide compares the ways to help, their advantages and their risks, and how to protect yourself.

Informational content, not legal or tax advice: consult a notary and an accountant. Each chapter ends with a lined “My notes” page.

More and more parents help their child get into homeownership. This lovely gesture deserves to be structured. This guide compares the ways to help — gift, family loan, co-signing — their advantages, their risks, and how to protect yourself.

Informational content, not legal or tax advice: consult a notary and an accountant.

chapters.title: The gift for the down payment
chapters.html:
Understanding the simplest option.

Gifting a sum for the down payment is common and accepted by lenders, provided you supply a gift letter confirming it isn't a repayable loan.

It's simple, but the money given is no longer yours. Two points of vigilance:

  • Consider fairness among your children (if you have several).
  • Think about the impact on your own retirement finances.

The down-payment gift is common and accepted by lenders, with a gift letter confirming it isn't repayable. Simple, but the money given is no longer yours: consider fairness among your children and the impact on your finances. Never empty your retirement cushion to help.

Emilie's tip

Never empty your retirement cushion to help a child. A generous gift that weakens you helps no one in the long run: help within what you can truly afford.

chapters.title: The family loan
chapters.html:
Lending rather than giving, cleanly.

You can lend rather than give to your child. In that case, put the terms in writing: amount, repayment, possible interest.

Careful: a loan to be repaid can affect the child's borrowing capacity and must be disclosed to the lender.

A poorly documented family loan is a classic source of misunderstandings: clarity protects the relationship.

You can lend rather than give: in that case, put the terms in writing (amount, repayment, possible interest). Careful, a loan to be repaid can reduce the child's borrowing capacity and must be disclosed to the lender. A poorly documented family loan is a classic source of misunderstandings.

Emilie's tip

Put the family loan on paper, even between parent and child. A simple document specifying “who owes how much, repaid how” avoids years of unspoken resentment.

chapters.title: Co-signing: helping without giving money
chapters.html:
Understanding a co-signer's real commitment.

By co-signing the mortgage, you help your child qualify thanks to your income and your credit. But the commitment is real:

  • You become responsible for the debt.
  • If the child doesn't pay, the lender can turn to you.
  • It appears in your credit file and affects your own borrowing capacity.

Co-signing isn't a mere courtesy signature: it's a full-fledged financial commitment.

By co-signing the mortgage, you help the child qualify thanks to your income and your credit — but you become responsible for the debt. If they don't pay, the lender turns to you, and it affects your own borrowing capacity. Only co-sign if you can truly bear it.

Emilie's tip

Never co-sign “just to help” without understanding that you're committing to the entire debt. If the child stops paying, it's you the bank will call. Sign only if you can bear it.

chapters.title: Protecting yourself while helping
chapters.objective: Helping in a way that protects everyone.
chapters.html:
Helping in a way that protects everyone.

Helping your child is a lovely gesture — one that deserves to be structured. A few reflexes protect the child and you:

  • Document systematically (gift letter or loan contract).
  • Consult a notary and an accountant on the legal and tax implications.
  • Plan for the case where the child's couple separates (especially if they buy together).

It's not a lack of trust: it's protecting the family relationship.

Helping deserves to be structured to protect everyone: document systematically (gift letter or loan contract), consult a notary and an accountant, and plan for the case where the child's couple separates (especially if they buy together). An agreement can protect the sum given.

Emilie's tip

If your child buys as a couple, think about what happens to your gift in the event of a separation. An agreement between partners can protect the sum you gave. The notary can guide you.

chapters.title: Choosing the right form of help
chapters.html:
Deciding with full knowledge.

Gift, loan, co-signing: each option has its logic. To choose:

  1. Clarify the form of help envisaged and your real capacity.
  2. Assess the impact on your own finances.
  3. Document it all (gift letter or loan contract).
  4. Consult a notary/accountant before committing.

Good help is the kind that moves the child forward without putting you at risk.

Gift, loan, co-signing: each option has its logic. To choose, clarify the form envisaged and your real capacity, assess the impact on your finances, document it, and consult before committing. Good help moves the child forward without putting you at risk.

Emilie's tip

There's no universal “best” option: it all depends on your situation. What matters is choosing with full knowledge, in writing, rather than on a whim.

chapters.title: Action plan
chapters.html:
Your next steps, concretely.

This week

  1. Clarify the form of help envisaged (gift, loan, co-signing).
  2. Assess the impact on my own finances.

Within 30 days

  1. Document the help (gift letter or loan contract).
  2. Consult a notary/accountant on the implications.

Next

  1. Help in a way that protects the child AND myself.

Before helping

  1. Clarify the form of help and assess the impact on my own finances.
  2. Document (gift letter or contract) and consult a notary/accountant.

chapters.title: Resources & glossary

• Gift letter: a document confirming that a gift isn't repayable.
  • Family loan: repayable help, to be documented in writing.
  • Co-signing: the parent's legal commitment on the child's mortgage.
  • Borrowing capacity: affected by a loan to be repaid or a co-signing.
  • Fairness among children: to consider when you help a single child.
